The Board · Special Report

Coffee to Kalshi

Thirty-three years ago, three engineers planned a company over diner coffee in San Jose. Tonight, a prediction market prices the founder’s exit by the day. The life, the company, and the week the two could not be separated.

By Josh Pilcher · Wednesday, November 11, 2026
Scroll

Santa Clara, California

The man is the company.

Thirty-three years, one chief executive, no successor. This week the market began pricing his exit.

Photograph via Invezz. Jensen Huang keynoting Nvidia’s GTC conference. The roadmap, the order book and the stock price are set from that stage, in one voice.

What’s Moved

The Wall Street Journal reports tonight that Nvidia’s board is preparing to remove Jensen Huang and could meet within days. No decision has been announced, no filing has been made, and he remains chief executive.

A second reported relationship, with a direct subordinate, moved the story from espionage adjacency to a plain conduct question under Nvidia’s own code, one the board can act on without any intelligence finding.

Kalshi’s exit ladder repriced violently on the Journal’s report: 64% gone before Friday, November 13, at 8:40 p.m. Eastern, up from about 37% hours earlier.

Nvidia shares fell 8.6% in after-hours trading Wednesday, to about $159, after losing about $430 billion of market value across Monday and Tuesday.

The forcing calendar is now set: earnings on November 17, a closed-door briefing before three House committees on November 18, and gavels in those committees that expire in January.

Verdict

Jensen Huang built Nvidia from a diner booth into the company the AI age runs on, and he built it so that no part of the company is separable from him. There is no successor, no number two, no chief operating officer. More than sixty executives report to him directly, the product roadmap lives in his keynote calendar, and the diplomacy that keeps the chips flowing was conducted by him in person, in Washington, Beijing, Riyadh and Taipei.

That is why a private scandal became a market event this week. On Sunday he admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, naming no one. American officials believe the woman identified in reporting as the other party, Alice Huang, was recruited by China’s intelligence service to target him. A newspaper now reports a second relationship, with his own subordinate. Tonight a prediction market prices him at 64% to be out of the job before Friday, and the stock has lost about $428 billion of market value in the two sessions that followed it.

The evidence does not establish that he spied, that he knew, or that anything was compromised. His board said on Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia’s secrets were compromised, and no charges exist against anyone. What is established is narrower, and for a board it may be enough: an admitted affair, a reported relationship with a direct report that the company’s own code treats as a conflict requiring disclosure, and a chief executive who is the single point of failure for a $4.2 trillion company.

Whether he goes will be decided by eleven directors, not by the crowd that set the price. But the price is now part of the decision, because every day it trades, it tells those directors what the world thinks their company is worth without him.

Chapter One

The Bet

A contract, a ladder of dates, and real money riding on whether one man keeps his job. The bet is the question. Everything after it is the answer.

Start with the bet, because the bet is the strangest document in this story.

On Kalshi, a regulated prediction exchange in the United States, there is a market titled “When will Jensen Huang leave as Nvidia CEO?” It is a ladder of dates. A contract pays out if he has actually left the job by that date. Announcing that he will leave later does not count. The departure has to happen.

At 8:40 p.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, the ladder read like this.

By later in the evening, Kalshi’s own page put the day’s trading at 10.3 million contracts. A different measure of the same frenzy.

The same exchange keeps a second price on the same man. In June, Kalshi’s market on the world’s second trillionaire made Huang the favorite, at prices as high as 50 cents on the dollar, on about $7,500 traded in the whole market. On Wednesday night that contract traded at 9 cents. One market says he is about to become the second richest person in human history. The other says he is about to be fired. Five months separate them.

Hold the discipline the rest of this report will keep. A prediction-market price is a price. It is not a probability measured by anyone with knowledge, and this market is three days old, thin at the front rungs, and moved 27 points on a single newspaper report on Wednesday evening. The after-hours stock, the perpetual futures, the rival exchange: all of them were trading on the same two newspaper stories. One signal, photocopied. The market’s design explains its violence. These contracts settle in cash, at one dollar or nothing, against an event with a public catalyst calendar: a reported board meeting, an earnings date, a testimony date. There is no dividend under the position and no hedge across it, and on a market three days old the book is thin enough that one motivated seller sets the quote the world then reads as a probability.

But a price this loud is itself a fact that needs explaining. Markets do not put a man’s job on a ladder of dates unless the man and the institution have become the same thing. Nobody trades a contract on when the chief executive of Exxon leaves, because Exxon would continue on Tuesday regardless. The bet exists because with Nvidia, nobody is sure that is true.

To understand the bet, you have to understand what is being priced. It is not a chip company. It is a life, thirty-three years long, that began in a diner booth over a bottomless cup of coffee.

Chapter Two

Coffee

A Baptist academy in Kentucky, a dish pit in Portland, and a booth in San Jose where three engineers planned a company on one bottomless coffee.

The booth is still there. It is a Denny’s on Berryessa Road in San Jose, California, and it carries a plaque that reads “The booth that launched a multi-trillion-dollar company.” The plaque was unveiled in September 2023, when the wording said a trillion. The number has had to be revised upward twice since.

Jensen Huang was born in Taiwan in 1963 and sent to America at nine, with his brother, to a school in Kentucky his aunt and uncle believed was prestigious. It was a Baptist academy for troubled boys. He lived in the dormitory, worked in it, and cleaned toilets. He taught his seventeen-year-old roommate to read in exchange for bench-press lessons, and learned table tennis from the man who filled the vending machines, well enough to become a nationally ranked junior player. His parents retrieved the boys after about two years. The family settled in Oregon, where the teenage Huang washed dishes at a Denny’s in Portland. The academy got its return in 2019, when he gave it $2 million for a dormitory and classroom building named Jen-Hsun Huang Hall and came back for the dedication. He took his electrical engineering degree at Oregon State in 1984, with highest honors, and a master’s at Stanford. He spent about a year at AMD designing microprocessors, then rose at LSI Logic to direct its CoreWare division. The LSI assignment that mattered was Sun Microsystems’ account: it is where he met Malachowsky and Priem. The founding team was a supplier relationship before it was anything else.

In late 1992 the three began meeting in the Berryessa Road booth, Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, two engineers from Sun Microsystems, planning a company in sessions that ran about four hours on one bottomless coffee. On February 17, 1993, his thirtieth birthday, Huang made it his first day of work. The idea was a chip built to do one thing at enormous scale: the three-dimensional graphics of video games. Sequoia Capital’s Don Valentine funded it on a pitch Huang himself says went badly. Nvidia was incorporated on April 5, 1993, with $40,000.

SCROLL

Its first product, the NV1, was what Huang himself calls a great technology achievement and a terrible product. A partner, Diamond Multimedia, shipped 250,000 units built around it and, by Diamond’s own account, took 249,000 back. The second product failed against a Microsoft standard Nvidia had bet against. Sega, the customer keeping the company alive, cancelled its contract. Huang flew to Japan and told Sega’s president, Shoichiro Irimajiri, that Nvidia could not finish the work and that he should hire another provider. Sega converted its final $5 million payment into an investment anyway. It is still the most consequential act of mercy in the history of the technology industry, and Huang has told the story for thirty years without varnish: he told Sega plainly that Nvidia could not do the work, and was funded instead.

The staff went from about a hundred people to about forty. What saved the company was the RIVA 128, in August 1997. Nvidia could not afford to build test chips, so the design was developed entirely in emulation, and the first working silicon came back right. It shipped a million units in four months. When it launched, the company had roughly a month of payroll in the bank.

Out of that year came the sentence Huang has run the company on ever since: our company is thirty days from going out of business. It is usually quoted as motivation. It is more useful read as architecture. A man who believes the firm is always thirty days from death does not build succession plans. He builds a company that cannot run a day without the person watching the clock. In 1997 that was a survival trait. The rest of this report is about what it became.

Chapter Three

The Long Winter

What a GPU actually computes, why neural networks eat matrix math, and the decade Wall Street hated the bet that made Nvidia inevitable.

In 1999 Nvidia shipped the GeForce 256 and named its category: the GPU, the graphics processing unit. The name was marketing. The technical substance was hardware transform and lighting: the geometry math of 3D scenes, until then run on the CPU, moved onto the chip. A GPU was not a faster graphics card. It was a re-division of labor inside the computer, and underneath it was a bet about what computing would become.

In 2000 Microsoft chose Nvidia to build the Xbox’s graphics chip and its audio and networking chipset, on a deal carrying a $200 million advance; within two years Xbox was about a fifth of Nvidia’s revenue, and within three the two companies were in binding arbitration. Microsoft, losing roughly $100 on every console, demanded lower chip prices. Nvidia answered that Microsoft had moved the design target repeatedly, that the engineering had cost far more than planned, and deferred the disputed revenue. An arbitration panel ordered Nvidia to keep supplying Microsoft’s reasonable requirements in September 2002. The settlement, in February 2003, put $40.4 million of recognized revenue into a single quarter. That August, ATI won the graphics for the next Xbox. The lesson was structural, and he never unlearned it: a platform owner squeezes its chip supplier on a schedule, and the supplier’s only lasting defense is a platform of its own.

A conventional processor, a CPU, is a small number of brilliant generalists. It does one complicated thing at a time, very fast. A GPU is the opposite: thousands of simple workers doing the same small operation at once. For games, the operation was shading pixels. The insight that made Nvidia is that the most valuable computation of the coming century has the same shape. Training a neural network is, at bottom, matrix multiplication: grids of numbers multiplied by grids of numbers, billions of times, with the backward pass that corrects the network costing roughly twice the forward pass that runs it. It is work for ten thousand line cooks, not ten chefs. Whoever owned the line cooks would own the era, if the era ever came.

In November 2006 Nvidia shipped CUDA, the software layer that let any programmer put the graphics chip to general work. The hardware had changed first. CUDA arrived with the GeForce 8800’s G80 chip, which replaced the separate fixed units for vertex and pixel work with 128 unified stream processors that could be pointed at any task, backed by shared memory and proper load and store. Unified shaders are the unglamorous fact underneath CUDA: for the first time, the graphics chip was a general-purpose computer that happened to draw. This was the bet Wall Street hated for a decade. CUDA cost real money every year and sold nothing directly. It existed so that researchers, engineers and eventually an industry would learn to think in Nvidia’s language: its compilers, its libraries for the core operations, its tools for making thousands of chips behave like one machine. For the four fiscal years ending in January 2013 through January 2016, company revenue stayed between $4.1 billion and $5.0 billion. After an early surge past 300,000 downloads in 2009, CUDA’s downloads then declined for three straight years. The winter was not a metaphor. It was a P&L.

The winter had a public face. Fermi, the architecture Nvidia shipped in 2010, ran at 250 watts and past 90 degrees, late and loud enough that AMD mocked it in an advertisement and frying an egg on a Fermi became the era’s joke. Fermi silicon is also what comes next: the GeForce GTX 580 in a Toronto bedroom was a Fermi card.

Then, on September 30, 2012, a team at the University of Toronto entered a neural network called AlexNet in the world’s main image-recognition contest. It was trained on two GeForce GTX 580 gaming cards, in Alex Krizhevsky’s bedroom at his parents’ house, the network split across the two cards because it did not fit on one. Its error rate was 15.3%. The best competing entry, built the traditional way, scored 26.2%. The field’s direction changed in a weekend. The hardware was necessary, not sufficient: AlexNet also needed Fei-Fei Li’s ImageNet dataset to learn from, and two algorithmic tricks, ReLU activations that made deep networks trainable at speed and dropout that kept them honest. And its software was one graduate student’s hand-written CUDA kernels. There was no cuDNN library until 2014 and no framework to call. The breakthrough ran on a platform, a dataset and a student’s code, in that order of permanence.

It changed on Nvidia hardware for a reason that had nothing to do with luck. The researchers used the only programmable platform available to them, and CUDA was the only programmable platform. Six years of winter spending had quietly made Nvidia the default instrument of a science that had not yet had its breakthrough. When the breakthrough came, it came pre-installed.

There is a pattern here that repeats at every scale of this story, and it is worth naming while it is still a virtue. Huang’s method is total concentration on a single judgment, held for years against the market’s advice, with no hedge and no deputy. In 2012 the judgment was about software. The winter made him look stubborn for six years and right in a weekend. Every later version of the same structure, including the one being priced tonight, runs on the credibility that weekend bought.

Chapter Four

The Delivery

A hand-carried machine, a networking company, and the moment the machine replaced the chip as the product. Plus the one empire he was not allowed to buy.

On an August day in 2016, Huang walked into the San Francisco office of a young research lab called OpenAI carrying a machine. The DGX-1 was a box with a $129,000 list price holding eight P100 accelerators wired together to act as one computer for training neural networks, 170 teraflops of it, at a moment when almost nobody outside a few labs believed training at that scale was a business. He signed the lid with a marker: “To Elon & the OpenAI Team! To the future of computing and humanity. I present you the world’s first DGX-1! Thanks, Jensen”

The delivery has hardened into legend, and the legend needs one correction from the record itself. Nobody wanted the machine, Huang likes to say. His own email to Elon Musk that April, filed in court this January, says the opposite: the DGX-1 was “selling itself off the web,” with demand “coming from all over” the world and orders already being taken for September. Both statements are in the record, and the tension between them is the truth. The delivery was theater. Theater was the strategy. The box was also distribution: a DGX was never a board for sale, it was the whole CUDA stack as an appliance, hardware and libraries and support in one unit, and every one that landed in a university lab trained the students who would staff the field to think in Nvidia’s language. He was not selling a server. He was anointing the customer who would define the decade, on camera, with a marker.

Underneath the theater, the product was changing shape. In 2017 the Volta generation added tensor cores, hardware that multiplies small grids of numbers in a single pass at deliberately reduced precision, because neural networks tolerate the sloppiness and reward the speed. In 2019 Nvidia agreed to pay $6.9 billion for Mellanox, the networking company whose switches let thousands of GPUs pool their memory and move like a single organism. The lesson of both moves is the same: the chip stopped being the product. The machine became the product, then the rack, then the building. In 2020 he tried to buy Arm, the architecture underneath nearly every processor on earth, for $40 billion, and abandoned the deal in February 2022 under regulatory pressure on three continents. It remains the one empire he was not permitted to buy.

By the end of the decade Nvidia sold the picks, the shovels, the mine and the railway. What it did not have, at any point, was a second person who could plausibly stand where Huang stood. The flat structure was already his signature: dozens of direct reports, no one-on-ones, no status meetings, the reasoning done in public in front of the whole room. It made the company fast and legible to exactly one mind. While the stock compounded quietly, nobody priced that. Pricing it was left to a stranger decade.

Chapter Five

The Folk Hero

Run, don’t walk. Pain and suffering as a benediction, a slogan that survives translation into arithmetic, and a management system with one seat.

On November 16, 2022, two weeks before ChatGPT existed in public, Huang told Nvidia’s investors that this was “the beginning of the era of generative AI.” When the era arrived on schedule, the world discovered the man in the leather jacket.

The folk-hero years, 2023 and 2024, are easy to mock and hard to argue with. He told graduates at National Taiwan University in May 2023 to run, don’t walk. He told Stanford students, at an economic summit in March 2024, “For all of you Stanford students, I wish upon you ample doses of pain and suffering,” and meant it as a benediction: resilience is not taught to people who succeed early. At Computex in Taipei, crowds followed him through night markets. At his own keynote that June, he sold the flagship machine, a rack of 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace processors, about 130 terabytes a second of bandwidth inside the rack and roughly 13.5 terabytes of fast memory, with a joke that became a slogan: “The more you buy, the more you save.”

The slogan survives translation into arithmetic, which is why it worked. A rack like that has been reported at a price in the low single-digit millions. The arithmetic works only while the racks stay busy: spread across the tokens it produces over its working life, the cost of each unit of intelligence falls as you buy more capacity, because the expensive thing in AI is not the chip, it is the idle chip. Huang himself supplied the honest footnote in the same keynote: “It isn’t accurate, but it is correct. CEO math.” The crowd was not being conned. It was being let in on the trade: his credibility was the collateral.

Underneath the rack sits the empire’s least visible constraint. Nvidia designs its chips; TSMC manufactures and packages them, and the packaging step that stacks high-bandwidth memory beside the processor, TSMC’s CoWoS, is the buildout’s narrowest gate: reported sold out through 2026, with lead times of a year or more, and Nvidia estimated to hold about 60% of the 2026 allocation. The thirty-year supply relationship at the center of the AI age runs, in Huang’s own repeated telling, without a contract.

The numbers underneath the fame were violent. Nvidia’s data-centre revenue went from $4.28 billion in the first quarter of its 2024 fiscal year to $47.5 billion for that year, on its way past $100 billion the next. The management system that produced it was now documented in public: his direct reports, more than forty in 2023, reached 55 by his own count in March 2024 and passed sixty by the time Stripe recorded him that year. No chief operating officer. No president. One pilot, sixty instruments, all wired to the same seat.

Hold that picture, because the folk-hero era is when the company’s greatest strength and tonight’s entire problem became the same fact. The system was not a failure of governance that nobody noticed. It was the product. Investors were not buying a chip roadmap with a charismatic salesman attached. They were buying the judgment of the man who had been right about CUDA for six winters and right about generative AI two weeks early, and they were paying a price that presumed the judgment would be on the premises indefinitely.

Chapter Six

The Statesman

The chip war made him a head of state: export lines drawn around his products, a revenue share negotiated with a president, and policy made in rooms he asked for.

The last transformation was from founder to head of state, and it happened because the product became a weapon system in the eyes of two governments.

In October 2022 Washington barred Nvidia’s best chips from China. Nvidia’s answer set the pattern for everything after: it designed the H800 to sit just under the legal line. When Washington closed that gap in October 2023, Nvidia answered with the H20, built to the new line. The H20 was the tell about how the game worked: a Hopper derivative with roughly a tenth of the H100’s computing power, sized to pass the rule, but with 96 gigabytes of HBM3 memory and 4.0 terabytes a second of bandwidth, more memory speed than the flagship. The rule measured computation. China’s inference workloads wanted bandwidth. Nvidia’s engineers found the seam between the regulation and the physics, and sold into it legally for a year. In April 2025 the administration required a licence for even the H20, indefinitely. Nvidia disclosed a charge of up to $5.5 billion tied to H20 inventory and purchase commitments, booked $4.5 billion of it in the first quarter, and said about $2.5 billion of H20 product went unshipped.

Huang’s response was diplomacy, conducted personally. Days after the April 2025 freeze he was in Beijing promising that Nvidia would “unswervingly serve” China. At Computex that May he called the export controls a failure, pointing out that they had cut Nvidia’s share of China’s AI-chip market from 95% to 50%. In June he and his lobbyists argued the case to the Deputy Secretary of State. In July he met the President, and the administration reversed the H20 ban. In August, Commerce issued the licences under an arrangement without precedent: 15% of the China sales revenue would go to the United States Treasury, according to contemporaneous reporting of the arrangement. The President said he had first sought 20% and accepted 15. On December 3, 2025, the GAIN AI Act, a bipartisan measure that would have put American customers first in line for advanced chips, was kept out of the annual defence bill after a lobbying push by Nvidia. Five days later the administration approved the more powerful H200 for China at a 25% federal cut.

Washington

The counterpart.

By 2025 the President of the United States was negotiating chip policy with him personally, and taking a percentage of the sales.

Photograph: The White House (Joyce N. Boghosian). Huang acknowledges the room at the White House AI Summit in Washington, July 23, 2025, as the President recognized him. The export-control regime’s most consequential private advocate, applauded in public by the state that wrote it.

On October 29, 2025, Nvidia became the first company in history worth $5 trillion. In December, Time named its Architects of AI, Huang among eight, and the Financial Times named him its Person of the Year, alone. Read the statesman years with the coldest eye available, because they are the years tonight’s allegations are about. Nothing in the record above establishes illegality. Designing to the legal line is what export law invites. Lobbying is legal. Negotiating with a president is what chief executives of strategic companies do. But notice what the structure required: the policy of the United States toward its principal rival, on the single most important technology of the decade, was substantially negotiated with one man, in rooms he asked for, on arguments he supplied. The state did not merely regulate Nvidia. It dealt with Huang as a counterpart. That is the fact the scandal now lands on, and it is why the scandal cannot be contained as a private matter even if every allegation about espionage turns out to be empty.

Chapter Seven

Texas

Foxconn in Houston, Wistron in Fort Worth, a grid queue measured in gigawatts. How close a fall in Santa Clara sits to a construction site in Texas: exactly one remove.

The empire acquired a Texas address in the same years, and the address is worth describing precisely, because precision is the only thing that separates a real local stake from a decorative one.

On April 14, 2025, Nvidia announced that its AI supercomputers would be manufactured in the United States: Foxconn building in Houston, Wistron in the Dallas area, packaging partners in Arizona, up to $500 billion of American AI infrastructure production through partners over four years. The Wistron plant turned out to be in Fort Worth. It opened on July 21, 2026: 324,000 square feet, $700 million invested, Nvidia’s GB300 systems in mass production and the next generation, Vera Rubin, slated to follow, with employment of more than 500 rising toward 1,000 by year end. Huang was on stage at the opening, and he signed the first unit. Foxconn’s Houston operation is running: Nvidia’s own update in August 2026 says the Houston plant builds GB300 tray modules, and Foxconn’s chairman said on October 30 that six Houston buildings are making Nvidia AI servers and that expansion is needed.

Underneath the factories sits the grid, and the grid is where Texas’s exposure actually lives. CenterPoint, which serves Houston, watched its data-centre interconnection queue go from about 1 gigawatt to 8 gigawatts in 2024 alone. By April 2026 12.2 gigawatts of industrial load was firmly committed in its queue, with 8 gigawatts of data-centre load expected to be energized by 2029 and 3.5 gigawatts already under construction. ERCOT, the state grid, set a demand record of 91,134 megawatts on July 22, 2026, and its interconnection queue holds roughly 474 gigawatts of requests, about 90% of them data centres, of which only about 9.5 gigawatts have been approved to energise. A queue is not demand: filing a wish cost almost nothing until the 2026 rules priced it, a $100,000 study fee plus posted security of $50,000 per megawatt, which is how wishes get separated from projects. The state’s politics moved before the scandal did: Senate Bill 6 in 2025 put large loads under new backup-power and curtailment rules, Governor Abbott demanded an audit of the queue on August 3, 2026 and lost the November 3 election to Gina Hinojosa, who takes office in January and repeated her call for a data-centre moratorium on November 5, three days before Huang’s admission letter. The one Texas load with Nvidia’s name on the hardware is Oracle’s campus at Abilene: 618 megawatts delivered by September 2026, about 131,000 Nvidia GPUs installed in a single quarter.

So how close is a fall in Santa Clara to a construction site in Fort Worth? Exactly one remove, and the remove has a name: order cadence. No contract in Texas runs through the chief executive’s chair. The buildings belong to Foxconn and Wistron, the Fort Worth tax abatement runs to Wistron, the jobs are Foxconn’s and Wistron’s, and CenterPoint’s load commitments are written against developers, not GPU vendors. What runs through Huang is Nvidia’s delivery schedule and its allocation decisions, because he built a company with no second signatory for either. If he falls and the GB300 systems ship on schedule, Texas gets a headline and nothing else. If deliveries slip by two quarters, the financing model that Texas fit-outs run on, debt raised against installed GPUs, pauses its draws, and CenterPoint’s energization dates slide with them. The factories would feel it first, because they sit closest to the cadence. Houston’s energy economy feels it one step later, through gas and power contracts sized to loads that arrive late. Texas representative Michael McCaul, the former Foreign Affairs chairman, read the same map on November 10 and called for a pause on advanced-chip shipments to China. He was not reacting to an affair. He was reacting to the discovery that the state’s largest new industrial bet and the country’s largest strategic exposure share a single point of failure, and that the point of failure is a person.

Chapter Eight

The Favorite

A fortune past $200 billion, a presidential medal, and a betting market installing him as the next trillionaire. The peak, complete, one month before the letter.

The peak, when it came, was total.

On May 13, 2026, the President took him to Beijing on the official delegation. On October 2, Forbes counted his fortune at $204.5 billion. On October 6 the stock closed at $239.24, its high. On October 8 he received the National Medal of Science. He had run the same company for thirty-three years, the longest tenure of any technology chief executive in the S&P 500, and the company was worth more than any company had ever been worth.

Between those bookends sits the detail that gives this report its title. On June 12, 2026, Elon Musk became the world’s first trillionaire on SpaceX’s stock-market debut. Three days later Kalshi opened a market on who would be second, resolving on the Forbes list, running to 2033. On June 23 the market made Huang the favorite at 50 cents. The honest footnote matters: the entire market had traded about $7,500 at that point, and CNBC’s contemporaneous read of the prices had him at 21%, behind Mark Zuckerberg. The favorite price was a postcard, not a poll. But postcards are what fame looks like from a distance. By the autumn of 2026, the reasonable summary of Jensen Huang’s position was that there was no position above his: the most valuable company, the indispensable product, a fortune past $200 billion, a medal from the president, and a betting market installing him as the next richest man alive.

A month later, on a Sunday, he published the letter.

Chapter Nine

The Week

A Sunday confession, a board reaching for outside counsel, a lawsuit filed minutes after Monday’s close, and five sets of stakes riding on one man. The week the empire priced its founder.

What he is accused of

The chronology arrives, as it had to, at the woman.

Alice Huang, as the record tonight can support it, had two careers. The first was in media and finance: a profile at Simuwang described a former CCTV journalist, a biography that Agence France-Presse could not verify and that a Hunan television executive has disputed; what is documented, by her former employer’s own posts reviewed by Reuters, is work at HSBC’s private bank and as a deputy general manager and executive director at Shanghai Hexi Asset Management in the middle of the last decade. The second career began in 2023, when she bought the Singapore arm of a Chinese gaming company, 7Road, renamed it Megaspeed, and served as its director and managing director from March to November of that year, before selling her stake and leaving its board.

Megaspeed’s business was renting computing capacity, built on Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian data centres, to Chinese technology giants including Alibaba. The allegation against it, maintained by American officials and denied by both Megaspeed and Nvidia, is diversion: that chips sold into the region reached China in violation of export law. Three money figures circulate and they must not be added together. American concern in 2024 centred on nearly $2 billion of purchases. Trade records reviewed by the New York Times show Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, buying $4.8 billion of Nvidia product between June 2024 and February 2026. The Information reported on November 10 that the relationship had “enabled the movement of” more than $7.5 billion of chips, an allegation about causation that no ledger in the public record supports as a sum. Her formal role at the company ended in November 2023. Most of the volume postdates it. No published source bridges that gap, and this report does not pretend otherwise.

The state’s file moved in parallel. The Bureau of Industry and Security developed concerns from 2024 and investigated, with little result. Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, then contacted the investigators to say that BIS’s own head, Jeff Kessler, had authorized the outreach. Officials regarded the approach as a protocol violation and suspected an attempt to pressure the case. The probe stalled, and in 2025 it moved to the Justice Department and the FBI, on the reported chronology, at which point Nvidia learned that it, and not only Megaspeed, was a subject. A highly classified State Department memorandum, drafted under Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s supervision and resting on electronic surveillance, warned senior policymakers that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to learn about American AI chips and possibly to influence Nvidia’s advocacy on China sales. One account dates the memo to the spring of 2025, another to the spring of 2026; it has not been published and the year is unverified. The President was briefed on it and took no action. Huang was never given a defensive briefing, the standard protective step for a targeted executive, and no source explains why.

The contact, on the record, was this. They reportedly met at a business lunch in Singapore in December 2023. They were seen at an Nvidia event in California in March 2024 and photographed together at Computex in June 2024. On May 22, 2025, at a Taipei restaurant during Computex, a camera recorded cheek kisses, his arm around her, and the two leaving in the same car. Photographs establish proximity and access. They establish nothing about content, and no named source in the public record establishes that Huang knew what American intelligence believed about her.

The publication cascade ran for a year before it reached him. The Times reported the intelligence conclusion about Alice Huang on October 29, 2026; Nvidia’s first response called the relationship not “unusual.” On November 4, the chairs of three House committees, on China, Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, asked him to brief them behind closed doors on November 18 and set November 11 for his answer. On November 6 the Times described the memo. On Sunday, November 8, Huang published his admission: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The same day, Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation led by independent directors with outside counsel, and said it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team” and had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” He would lead, the statement said, “without interruption.”

On Monday the lawsuit arrived: *Kistenmacher v. NVIDIA*, filed in federal court in San Jose, alleging that Huang and the company violated Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act by concealing the relationship, and its national-security risk, while making the reassuring statements that had propped the price; Huang alone faces a control-person claim under Section 20(a). The class period runs from October 9, 2025, the first Megaspeed story, to November 8, 2026, the admission. The same day, the President, asked on camera about the case, called Huang “an honorable guy” and a “fine person,” and, of the espionage allegation, said Huang had told him he had “absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” adding: “I really believe him.” The stock fell 4.3%.

On Tuesday the board retained Wachtell Lipton, the law firm of record for corporate America in a crisis, with the investigation run by Joon H. Kim, a former acting US Attorney. The stock fell another 5.5%, its second straight loss, to $168.89. Across the two sessions about $430 billion of market value disappeared.

Wednesday brought the two stories that changed the question. The Times reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare and Huang’s direct report, sourced to five unnamed current and former Nvidia employees; two described a hotel video the Times has not seen, no party has confirmed the account, and Reuters could not verify it. Treat it as what it is: an allegation. Then the Wall Street Journal reported that the board is preparing to oust him and could meet as soon as Wednesday to decide. No decision has been announced. In after-hours trading on Wednesday, after the Journal’s report, the stock fell another 8.6%, to about $159. As this report publishes, Jensen Huang remains the chief executive of Nvidia. No charges exist against Huang, against Alice Huang, or against Megaspeed. That sentence is fact, and everything around it should be read in its light.

Why the second story matters more than the first

The espionage story, even at its worst sourced version, runs into the board’s own finding: no reason to believe anything was compromised, and no evidence in the public record that Huang knew what the intelligence agencies believed. Unwitting targets are victims in American law and in most boardrooms.

The Powell report is different in kind, and the difference is mechanical. Nvidia’s own code of conduct lists a personal relationship with a subordinate as a conflict of interest requiring preapproval and recusal. No waiver or disclosure appears in the company’s filings. If the report is true, the board does not need a single classified fact to act: it has a documented rule, a direct report, and a chief executive who did not disclose. The precedents sort themselves by exactly this distinction. The founders who survived scandal, at Meta and Amazon, were accused of many things but never of a concealed relationship with a subordinate inside their own reporting line. The executives who fell fastest, at Intel and BP, fell on precisely that fact pattern, and both were replaceable managers. Huang is not replaceable. That is the board’s problem stated in one line: the fact pattern that ends tenures belongs to the one tenure the market believes cannot end.

The board’s problem

Strip the drama and the governance arithmetic is this. Nvidia has eleven directors and no chairman; Stephen C. Neal, the lead independent director since 2019, chairs the committee that nominates the others. Every director is elected annually. There is one class of stock. Huang owns 3.6% of it, about 871 million shares as of the March 2026 proxy. The board may remove him by majority vote, with or without cause. Nvidia’s executives serve at will, and the company keeps no severance agreements that would tax the decision. On paper, eleven people can end the Jensen Huang era before lunch, for free.

The directors’ own exposure runs the other way, and it is why waiting is not free either. Under Delaware’s Caremark doctrine, directors breach their duty of loyalty if they make no good-faith effort to monitor a risk central to the business, or consciously ignore red flags once they see them. A board that now knows of an undisclosed conflict at the top of its company, and of its own code’s preapproval rule, and does nothing visible, has written the oversight claim that follows the securities suit in every modern scandal. In practice every route is expensive, and the expense is the story. Analyst Dan Ives put the founder’s premium at 25% to 30% of the company’s value, while putting his own odds of removal at about 15%. His arithmetic, multiplied out, is almost exactly what the market did on Monday: 15% of a 25% to 30% loss is a 4% stock decline, and the stock fell 4.3%. The market is not pricing certainty. It is pricing a probability, and repricing it with every headline.

The routes, and what each one costs. Clean removal this week requires a successor by morning, and the bench is the problem the flat system built: the clearest same-day interim candidate is the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, because sixty executives with deep narrow mandates do not add up to one chief executive. A negotiated exit, a dated transition announced as his decision, preserves the founder’s narrative and the stock’s dignity, but the Kalshi contract’s terms expose its limit: an announced future departure does not settle the bet, and more importantly does not settle the question of who runs the company in the interval while three investigations run. A president installed over him, the smaller cage, keeps the roadmap and the keynotes while stripping the diplomacy and the China book; it is the containment option and it concedes, in writing, that the old structure is over. Survival unchanged is the cheapest route on Tuesday’s prices and the most expensive if the Wachtell investigation, which is charged with answering whether he was targeted and whether anything was compromised, returns an answer the board has not pre-cleared. The investigation’s own logic constrains the calendar: a credible probe runs four to six weeks on Ives’ estimate, which means a findings-driven decision by Friday is not available. Whatever happens this week happens on governance grounds, the Powell fact pattern and the code, or it does not happen on evidence at all.

Two dates now force the board’s hand regardless of its preference. Earnings arrive on November 17, when Huang either fronts the call as the unquestioned chief executive or does not. On November 18 he is expected behind closed doors in Room 2172 of the Rayburn Building, where the Intelligence Committee’s chairman can compare his answers against the classified record the Gang of Eight was briefed on November 9. A closed door is not a safe room: false statements to Congress carry federal exposure whether or not the cameras are present, and a referral from that room is the one product of the hearing that outlives this Congress, whose gavels expire in January. The chairman of Foreign Affairs has already said the word subpoena on the record.

The five stakes

For Huang, the week is priced in his own paper. Forbes counted $204.5 billion on October 2. At Monday’s close the same stake was worth $155.4 billion. The difference between his three exits is not money, since no outcome restores the stock, but standing. Removal makes the ending a verdict. Resignation on a negotiated date makes it a retirement. Survival in a smaller cage makes it a diminution he would have to perform in public, at keynotes, for years. And over all three hangs the question no board controls: what the investigation he cannot see, run by the FBI and the Justice Department since 2025, eventually says about the years when a woman his government believed was an intelligence asset had his ear.

For Nvidia, the exposure runs through channels that can be named. The succession vacuum is the first, and it is now a traded price rather than a governance footnote. China is the second, but not in the way it is usually told: China revenue has already fallen from 19.2% of the total in fiscal 2025 to single digits, 5.2% in the quarter to October 2025 and 8.2% in the latest filed quarter, so the stake is not current sales, it is the licence regime and the option value of the market he spent two years negotiating open. The Megaspeed channel is the third: the entity list, Washington’s main tool, has had no additions in more than a year, the most investigated suspected diverter in the system is not on it, and every intermediary in Southeast Asia can read that ceiling. The fourth is the diplomacy book: the sovereign deals, Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN at 500 megawatts and 18,000 GB300 chips, the Gulf’s G42 at 35,000 chip-equivalents, were negotiated with Huang personally. The chips are under contract. The relationships were not. The supply machine is the exception that proves the structure: it has a named operator, Debora Shoquist, who has run operations since 2009 and holds the TSMC and packaging allocation book. Deliveries have a second signature. Diplomacy does not.

For shareholders, the lawsuit’s theory is narrower than the headlines. Securities law does not compensate a stock’s whole fall; it compensates the inflation removed by a corrective disclosure, which plaintiffs will identify with November 9’s 4.3% decline, and the securities law’s bounce-back rule measures recovery against the stock’s average price over the ninety days after disclosure. Settlements at this scale settle for a small fraction of even that measure, historically in the region of 1% to 1.5% of estimated investor losses, which puts a realistic outcome in the hundreds of millions, not the trillions of the peak-to-trough arithmetic. The deeper point is structural. Nvidia is about 6.9% of the S&P 500 on some measures (6.3% of SPY on November 10) and 7.1% of QQQ. The great mass of its holders are index funds that cannot sell a constituent for being scandalous, and long-only managers benchmarked too tightly to leave. This week’s price was therefore set by the marginal fast-money trader and marked, instantly, across a base of owners who never transacted. The same mechanism runs violently in reverse if he is cleared. The price is not a verdict on the company’s cash flows. It is a probability, marked to a hostage base.

For the United States, the implications split on the same fact the investigation exists to settle. If he was compromised, the policy record of 2025 becomes retrospectively suspect: the H20 reversal, the 15% and then 25% revenue shares, the GAIN AI Act kept out of the defence bill on December 3, 2025, the H200 approval five days later. Suspicion does not void those licences; no mechanism in administrative law runs backwards like that. What it does is reclassify the record as counterintelligence evidence and reverse the burden on the next approval, where proposals like the AI OVERWATCH Act would make Commerce certify, in advance, that a licensee’s exports will not be diverted, including through rented compute. Before this week, declining to certify was a hawk’s preference. After it, certifying means Commerce vouching personally for a company whose chief executive is under FBI investigation. If, instead, he was merely targeted and careless, the finding is structural and survives his exoneration: the country’s AI lead, as administered, had a single point of failure in three layers at once. One vendor supplied the chips the rules were written around. That vendor’s chief executive was the regime’s most effective private advocate, with personal access to the President. And the one government mechanism built for exactly this case, the defensive briefing, was never used on him, while the President was briefed and took no action. A hostile service did not create that concentration. It only had to find it. The dependence underneath is real but specific: a $500 billion domestic buildout with Nvidia as anchor tenant, the Energy Department’s Solstice and Equinox machines. It is not fiscal. The H200 licences have produced no revenue, and the H20 licences roughly $60 million. Washington does not need Nvidia’s money. It needs Nvidia’s machines.

For AI itself, the striking fact is how much does not move. The supply chain is locked two to four quarters deep: packaging queues run a year or more, and Nvidia’s filings show $279 billion of supply commitments inside $366 billion of total commitments. A shock in November 2026 lands physically in the delivery allocations of 2028. The scoreboard of the other Board report, America’s fleet of accelerators at 23 million H100-equivalents against China’s 880,000, does not change on any horizon shorter than eight quarters, because China’s constraints are lithography and memory yields, and neither runs through a chief executive in Santa Clara. CUDA survives him without argument: its maintenance is institutional, spread across the organizations of the men who built it, six million developers and the default settings of every major framework. What dies with him is narrower and, for the buildout, more immediate: the allocation discretion, the keynote calendar that repriced a $500 billion order book in October 2025 and a $1 trillion one in March 2026, and deals struck on his word, like OpenAI’s ten-gigawatt letter of intent of September 2025, whose first Vera Rubin gigawatt is due in the second half of 2026. The field’s infrastructure is sturdier than its figurehead. Its schedule was his voice.

One discipline note before the close, because this week will be misread without it. The Kalshi ladder, the rival exchange’s market, the after-hours stock and the perpetual futures are not four confirmations of anything. They are one signal, the Journal’s report and the Times’s report, photocopied across four screens. The climate underneath has not changed since Tuesday: a board that has publicly pre-cleared its founder on the compromise question, an investigation with no timetable, and a second allegation that has ended lesser tenures on its own. Weather is loud. Bet on climate at your own risk.

Chapter Ten

What Happens Next

Possibilities, offered as possibilities. Two reads that divide the field, what would decide between them, and what the prices say the crowd believes.

Pose the question plainly, because the report exists to answer it. What happens next?

The honest answer is a field of possibilities, and the discipline is to keep them labelled as possibilities. Some rest on logic: what eleven directors can and cannot make themselves do, what findings would force their hands, what a closed-door room on November 18 changes. Some rest on the market: the ladder is the crowd’s priced possibility set, and each rung says something specific. The Dec 1 rung, at 84%, says the crowd believes this resolves within weeks, one way or the other; stasis is the outcome the market prices least. The long rungs moved furthest of all: the contract on his departure before 2031 traded at 16 cents a week ago, on almost no volume, and stood at 94 cents by late Wednesday. Nobody prices him dying in the job any more. The era in which Jensen Huang’s tenure was a permanent feature of the world ended this week, whatever the board decides.

Two of the possibilities are coherent enough to be called reads, and they divide the field between them.

Read One

The board holds

The board that investigated its founder on Sunday and announced confidence in the same statement was not performing surprise; it was stating a position it had the intelligence reporting to inform. Wachtell gives the board a record on which eleven directors can say, in January, that they examined the worst and found a targeted man, not a compromised one, and the Powell allegation, unconfirmed by any second outlet, gets absorbed into a governance settlement: a president or chief operating officer installed beneath him, a strengthened lead director, recusal from China decisions, a conduct framework with his case as its unnamed exhibit. The precedents that govern are the founder precedents. Zuckerberg survived worse headlines because the alternative was unthinkable to his board. Huang’s board is loyal, long-tenured, and aware that firing him costs the shareholders a quarter of the company on Dan Ives’ arithmetic, even though Ives himself puts the odds of removal at only about 15%. Under this read, November 13 passes with no filing, the ladder collapses back toward where it sat before the Journal’s story, and he fronts the earnings call on November 17 as the chastened but standing chief executive of Nvidia.

Decide by: November 13 passes with Huang in office and no 8-K filed. The board reaffirms him, or lets the investigation’s timeline stretch publicly past the November 17 earnings call. Huang fronts the call and takes hostile questions standing up. Or the containment furniture appears: a president, a strengthened lead director, a recusal from China decisions, because furniture is what survival looks like when it is being built.

Read Two

The board is already moving

Boards do not retain Wachtell Lipton in a crisis to write a valentine. The leak to the Journal came from somewhere with knowledge of the board’s deliberations, and its function was to prepare the market and the man. The board does not need the espionage allegation at all: the Powell report, if corroborated, hands it a documented conduct violation under its own code, with no disclosed waiver, involving the one man whose personal conduct is the company’s central risk. It cannot send him into a classified briefing on November 18, seven days from now, as the company’s face while its own lawyers are still asking whether he was compromised; the committees’ gavels expire in January, and every institutional actor in Washington has the same incentive to settle this while the settling is theirs to control. Under this read, the announcement comes before the earnings call, framed as his decision or as a mutual one, with Colette Kress as interim and a search announced the same morning. The stock loses its founder premium in a single session and then, on the precedent of Jobs’s resignation and Buffett’s succession, discovers that the cash flows were less personal than the multiple was.

Decide by: Nvidia files an 8-K, or issues any statement containing the words transition, interim or leave, before November 17. A second outlet corroborates the Powell relationship with named or documentary sourcing. Or any of the three committee chairs announces a subpoena, which converts a briefing into a custody fight over the witness.

What would decide between them is observable, and soon. Each read carries its own executioners.

The wider field sits around those two. A Wachtell leak reporting that he knew of the intelligence interest and concealed it from his board would end the argument in an afternoon; concealment from the board is the one fact pattern that unifies directors who agree on nothing else. A Justice Department move against Huang personally, as opposed to the company or the intermediaries, would take the decision out of the boardroom entirely, and nothing in the public record tonight says it is coming. Beijing, which has already blocked the legal chip channel and was already substituting away from Nvidia, gains its cheapest victory if Washington destroys its own advocate for engagement without Beijing lifting a finger. And there is the possibility nobody prices because it has no drama: that the week simply continues, earnings land, the testimony happens behind its closed door, the investigation runs its four to six weeks, and the ladder’s front rungs expire worthless one date at a time while the man does the job. The market gives that outcome about one chance in six before December. This report offers no better number. It offers the deciders above, and notes that they are all dated within the next thirty days.

Chapter Eleven

Watchlist

Five dated things. Each one settles an argument made above.

  • 1Any 8-K filing or Nvidia newsroom statement. The decision, when it exists, will exist here first. A filing before November 17 means the board has moved on governance grounds; silence through Friday is itself the strongest early evidence for containment.
  • 2The November 17 earnings call. Who hosts it, whether Huang takes questions, and whether the guidance language changes. A founder fronting his own crisis call, unscripted, is what survival looks like. An absent or armoured Huang is a transition already in progress.
  • 3November 18, Room 2172. Whether he appears, and what the chairs say afterward. The word to listen for is referral: it is the only output of a closed-door briefing that transfers the file to an institution whose clock does not expire in January.
  • 4The Wachtell investigation’s first leak. The probe is charged with two questions, targeted and compromised. The finding that ends the debate is neither. It is evidence that Huang knew of the intelligence interest and kept it from his board. Watch for reporting about knowledge and concealment, not about espionage.
  • 5Washington’s entity list. Whether Megaspeed is listed, after a freeze of more than a year. A listing means the state has begun repricing its own exposure and dismantling, in public, the policy era Huang negotiated. Continued silence, while his case is the most documented in the system, tells every intermediary in Southeast Asia where the ceiling still is.

Kalshi, tonight.
